item.title: Sovereign models are an architectural choice
item.dc:creator: Martin Callaghan
item.description:
It is tempting to treat a locally hosted model as a sovereign model. Local inference matters, but sovereignty concerns control across the whole system: models, data, infrastructure, dependencies and operating knowledge.

Think in dependencies

A useful assessment begins with a dependency map rather than a model leaderboard.

Layer Questions
Model Can the weights and licence support the intended use?
Data Where do training, retrieval and evaluation data reside?
Runtime Which proprietary services, drivers or accelerators are required?
Operations Can the system be monitored, repaired and upgraded locally?
Governance Who can inspect its evidence, decisions and changes?

A system may be locally deployed while remaining operationally dependent on opaque components. Conversely, a carefully governed hosted component might be compatible with an organisation’s actual sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty is contextual

There is no single threshold at which a system becomes sovereign. The relevant degree of control depends on the risk, jurisdiction, continuity requirements and sensitivity of the task.

TipA more useful design question

Ask which dependencies must remain under whose control—and what happens when each external dependency disappears.

This turns sovereignty from a slogan into a set of testable architectural requirements.

item.title: What does intelligence engineering include?
item.dc:creator: Martin Callaghan
item.description:
A capable model is not yet a capable system. Between a prompt and a dependable outcome sit choices about data, adaptation, retrieval, tools, evaluation and deployment.

This site uses intelligence engineering as an umbrella for those choices.

A provisional stack

A useful way to organise the territory is into six interacting layers:

  1. Models — capability, size, modality and licence.
  2. Adaptation — prompting, fine-tuning and preference optimisation.
  3. Context — retrieval, memory, knowledge graphs and tools.
  4. Orchestration — workflows, agents and decision policies.
  5. Assurance — evaluation, observability, provenance and safety.
  6. Operations — latency, cost, privacy and sovereign deployment.

The layers are not a maturity model. More machinery is not necessarily better. A small model with constrained outputs and a well-designed retrieval layer may outperform a much larger general model for a defined task.

NoteWorking principle

Treat model selection as one architectural decision among several—not as the architecture itself.

Questions worth asking

When examining a new technique, I find these questions more useful than asking whether it is impressive:

  • What decision or transformation is the system meant to support?
  • Where does its relevant knowledge come from?
  • Which claims can be traced to evidence?
  • What happens when the evidence is incomplete or contradictory?
  • What is the smallest sufficient model and architecture?
  • How will failure be detected outside a demonstration?

Future articles will test and revise this map. It is a starting point, not a settled taxonomy.
